notes.meaning: Abimelech was one of Gideon's sons. Jerubbaal is Gideon's other name. Right after his father died, he went to Shechem, his mother's hometown, hungry for power. He started with his mother's family. One commentary sees here the harm of having many wives: this son had family ties and interests quite apart from his brothers'.

Abimelech planted a lie. He hinted that Gideon's seventy sons planned to rule over Shechem together. In fact Gideon had refused to be king, and nothing shows his sons wanted to rule. Abimelech judged his brothers by his own greed for power. "Your own flesh and blood" simply means "I am your relative."

His uncles passed the message on, and the leaders of Shechem were won over. "He is our brother" really meant "his rise will be good for us." They pictured their city as the capital and themselves in top jobs. Shechem was an important city, where Joshua had held his last great meeting with Israel.

The money came from the temple of Baal-berith, an idol whose name means "god of the covenant." The temple held the city's treasure. Adam Clarke says a work begun with an idol's money is not likely to end to God's glory. Abimelech used it to hire worthless, reckless men who had nothing to lose.

Abimelech killed his brothers "on one stone." This was a planned, formal killing. Some think it may have been done on an altar, as revenge for Gideon tearing down Baal's altar. Seventy is a round number, since Jotham, the youngest, hid and escaped. Matthew Henry notes how selfish ambition can tear apart even the closest family love.

No one asked God whether they should have a king, let alone this man. Instead of punishing a murderer, Shechem crowned him. They did it by the oak and memorial stone, the very spot where Joshua had renewed Israel's covenant with the Lord. Beth-millo probably means the people of the city's fortress. Abimelech was the first man in Israel to take the title "king," which Gideon had turned down.

Jotham climbed Mount Gerizim, the mountain where Israel had once spoken blessings. It rises steeply right over Shechem, so his voice could carry to the people below. "May God listen to you" means: if you want God to hear your prayers, first hear me out. His words sound like the words of a prophet.

Jotham told a story about trees choosing a king. It is the oldest such story we know. Matthew Henry says the trees had no need of a king, just as Israel didn't, because the Lord was their King. They asked the olive tree first, since it was the most useful tree of all.

Olive oil honored God in offerings and in the lamps of worship. It honored people when kings and priests were anointed with it. "Hold sway" carries the idea of waving or swaying to and fro. It pictures trading a settled, fruitful life for the restless worry of ruling.
The fig tree gave the same kind of answer. Its fruit was famous for its sweetness. Ruling would cost it that sweet, fruitful life. Matthew Henry says good people would rather be useful than great.

The vine refused too. Wine "cheers God" in the sense that God was pleased when offerings were accepted, and wine was poured out at the altar. All three good trees refused to rule. This pictures Gideon and other good people turning down the crown.
At last "all the trees" agreed to ask the thornbush. A thornbush bears no fruit and only scratches whoever comes near. In the end it is good for nothing but burning. It stands for Abimelech.

The thornbush's reply drips with irony. It gives almost no shade, and anyone who shelters under it just gets scratched. Thorns catch fire easily, though. A worthless man can still bring harm on the greatest people, the "cedars," meaning the city's leading men.

Now Jotham applies the story. Gideon had risked his life to save them from Midian. They repaid him by killing his sons and crowning "the son of his maidservant," a phrase meant as a put-down. Jotham blames Shechem for the murders too, because they paid for them.

"If you did right, enjoy your king!" These are words of bitter scorn, because Jotham knew they had not done right. He leaves the outcome to God's providence, meaning God's guiding hand over events. Time would show who was in the wrong.

Jotham's curse is that Abimelech and Shechem will destroy each other. Partners in evil end up as a plague to one another. Later in the chapter it comes true, even down to the fire that burns the city's tower.
After speaking out, Jotham ran for his life. He went to Beer, a common place name meaning "well." He lived there in hiding, afraid of his brother.

The word for "reigned" here suggests a tyrant's rule, not a judge's gentle, God-given leadership. He ruled over only part of Israel, those who would accept him. His power lasted just three years. The success of the wicked is short.

This was God's just punishment for the murder of Gideon's sons. Older commentators explain it a little differently. Some say God let jealousy and distrust grow as a punishment. Others say he let an evil spirit stir up trouble, or handed them over to their own evil desires. Either way, God is not the author of their sin, but the punishment comes from him. Those who helped with the crime are held guilty along with the killer.

Shechem's men lay in wait on the hills, maybe hoping to catch Abimelech himself. They robbed travelers too, which made Abimelech look unable to keep the roads safe. One commentator thinks they were also taking the tolls he collected from traders. Abimelech heard about it.

Nobody knows much about Gaal. He seems to have led a roving band and was probably of Canaanite stock. The unhappy men of Shechem put their hope in him. Matthew Henry calls it one thornbush fighting another.

At the grape harvest they held a festival in the temple of their idol. Over food and wine they cursed Abimelech. It was the same temple whose money had once put him in power. They turned on their king but kept their idol.

Gaal mocked Abimelech as the son of Jerubbaal, the man who tore down Baal's altar. He mocked Zebul, the officer Abimelech had put over the city. He urged them to serve "the men of Hamor," the old Canaanite family that founded Shechem. Gaal didn't want to free the city. He only wanted to swap one tyrant for another.
